entries.description: Operator set pathAwareCritique: advisory.

Registered S1 via start_session (claude/anthropic/claude-opus-5/high); read the preload, the spec, and the Session Set Configuration block. Confirmed the operator precondition: the published answer key resolved HEAD=2acc7b7 via git ls-remote, matching the local reference solution's master. No placeholder URL is inherited.

Extracted both service contracts as LITERAL wire bodies from a real run rather than by reading source: started converter (:5101) and persistence (:5102) from the reference solution and captured POST /convert 200 + 400 (bad file, unknown schema), GET /schemas, POST /batches 201 + 200-duplicate + 400, and GET /batches/{id}. Recorded in s1-service-contracts.md with the capture recipe.

Settled Part D by PROVING it, with a falsifier. Started a second converter on :5201 alongside :5101 (both healthy at once); repointed the watcher by configuration only (Watcher__Converter__BaseAddress), no code edited or rebuilt; processed a CSV end to end; then KILLED the converter on :5101 and confirmed the pipeline still worked. All four decision-table rows forced live (Stored / AlreadyStored / Rejected / Deferred), including a deferred file retried and stored on a later tick. Port allocation fixed at 51xx=yours, 52xx=the version you test against. Recorded that this proves the repoint MECHANISM, not cross-implementation conformance (same build on both ports).

Settled layout and naming via a two-engine decision consult (gpt-5-4 + gemini-pro, bias-cautions preamble, raw in s1-layout-naming-consensus.json). decision_consensus.enabled is false repo-wide; the consult was run per the spec's instruction without touching the config flag. Both engines converged on owner-in-slug, so the result was synthesized rather than escalated. Ruled: slug {owner}-{service}, title {Service} ({Owner}), code root modules/{owner}/{service}, member-major manifest order, one CODEOWNERS line per member. This REVISES the spec's POC recommendation (converter-v1): version-in-slug stays unique only with central version allocation, contradicting 'nobody waits on anybody'.

Confirmed the POC's four findings against the RUNNING PRODUCT, not just the model functions. Authored src/test/poc-nine-modules-ondisk.ts: writes a real nine-module workspace to disk and drives classifyModulesManifest -> readSessionSets -> computeVisibleModules -> buildVisibleModulePayloads (the payload the shipping renderer receives since Set 092). 5 passing: nine declared rows from the product's own parser and discovery; grouping exactly one level deep with no per-member tier; manifest order beats alphabetical (with a guard that the fixture actually distinguishes them); day-one nine-empty renders warning-free; and the version-slug collision condition pinned as an assertion. Re-ran the original poc-nine-modules.ts: 4 passing.

Routed an analysis (task_type=analysis, excl. anthropic -> gemini-2.5-pro) of the draft outline against the concept-ownership table, adopt-dabbler.md and hello-world.md. Raw in s1-outline-ownership-review.json. One Critical accepted whole (the prerequisite list omitted the reader's entry state - they would stall on instruction one; R8 split into R8a entry state and R8b build installs). One Major accepted as a real hazard but REJECTED as a fix: it asked R4 to link to adopt-dabbler.md Part 5, which Session 3 deletes; R4 now records the transfer plus a hard S2-writes-before-S3-deletes ordering constraint.

Wrote s1-walk-outline.md: rulings R1-R8b, the four parts with independent finish lines, the single happy path, the ownership table, and the handover to Sessions 2/3/4. Also recorded R8b, a factual correction to the spec's prose: the success criterion's 'nothing but the .NET 10 SDK' is false - LocalDB is a separate MSI product (verified against this machine's installed-products registry) and there is no winget package for it alone. Flagged for the operator; the spec assigned this to Session 4, which is too late because Session 2 writes the prerequisite list.

Build and test. Reference solution: dotnet build succeeded (SDK 10.0.201, pinned by global.json). Extension unit suite via the vscode-stub mocha path: 1821 passing. pytest: see the verification conventions block for the recorded baseline.

Registered S2 via start_session (claude/anthropic/claude-opus-5/high). Read the four preload files, the spec (Session Set Configuration block: full tier, requiresUAT true, requiresE2E false, uatStyle ad-hoc, uatScope per-set, pathAwareCritique advisory) and the S2 plan. Decision-review-queue: absent, nothing to triage.

Confirmed S1 Creates exist and are non-empty: s1-service-contracts.md (both contracts as literal captured wire bodies) and s1-walk-outline.md (rulings R1-R9, four parts, ownership table, handover). Read both in full plus s1-conventions.md. S1 closed VERIFIED; answer key published at github.com/darndestdabbler/dabbler-ai-orchestration-multimodule-demo, so there is no placeholder to inherit.

Wrote docs/tutorials/three-module-pipeline.md (1229 lines) against s1-walk-outline.md, holding R1-R9 as settled. Four parts, each with a behavioural finish line and a Coming-back-to-this state block. No declaration step in Parts A/B/C (R9 owns declaration). Answer key linked by its real published URL; no placeholder written.

Part D written as the payoff: two configuration values, no code change, one machine, localhost throughout. Per-member database via the ConnectionStrings__Orders environment override, so a teammate service runs without editing any file in their code root. Solo limitation stated plainly (two copies of one build prove the repoint mechanism, not cross-implementation conformance). Cross-machine variant is appendix-only with the firewall step marked unverified.

Re-established the quotable literals by RUNNING the reference solution today rather than trusting the S1 transcription: dotnet --list-sdks, sqllocaldb info, the full dotnet test summary (31/24/19 = 74) and the Phase A decision-table filter (12 tests, 81 ms). Wrote a checker (scratchpad/check_literals.py) that extracts every wire-body / test-summary line from the tutorial and fails unless it appears verbatim in a provenance source: 14/14 traceable. It caught one fabrication in my own draft - a Stored transcript whose fileName I had changed while keeping the real batchId - which was removed.

Mechanical duplication scan over twelve procedure phrases owned by other documents (Marketplace, Install ai-router, branch protection, git clone, venv/pip, Copilot CLI, Delete Module, approval settings): zero hits. New Module appears once, as a named link-out to adopt-dabbler Part 3, not as an explanation.

Routed two off-provider reviews (anthropic excluded). (1) Duplication / ownership / S3-fragility review vs the pre-trim adopt-dabbler.md, hello-world.md and release-and-recovery.md -> s2-duplication-review.json: one Major S3-fragility (the touches: passage cited the app/greeter example that lives in adopt-dabbler Part 5, which S3 deletes - the reference would dangle), two Minor broken handoffs (Parts 1-2 should be Part 1; Part 3 should be Parts 2-3), one Minor duplication. All four acted on. (2) Documentation review against ten named rules incl. host-neutrality -> s2-documentation-review.json: 9/10 pass, one Major on the mkdir commands.

DISMISSED the documentation review Major as stated, on evidence: it claimed creating a folder at the root of C: needs administrator rights and that mkdir is not recursive. Probed both on this machine in a non-elevated PowerShell - mkdir C:\<new>\incomingrchive succeeded and created the intermediate folder, so both stated mechanisms are false, and its proposed fix would have put an unexpandable ~/Documents path into appsettings.json. Kept the residual (a locked-down managed workstation could still refuse) and fixed it by REMOVAL per the simplicity-first convention: three mkdir lines collapsed to two, plus one sentence saying any writable folder works.

Ran verify_session --phase discovery (fan-out 2, all severities) with s2-conventions.md as the up-front conventions block. Round 1 returned ISSUES FOUND: six Majors, five nits. The raw artifact s2-verification.md was written, but a 10-minute harness timeout killed the process before it could write s2-issues.json or patch disposition.json - so the paid verifier output survived (artifact-first write order, L-079-1) while the findings envelope did not. Both --phase supplementary and --phase remediation-review refuse to run without that envelope, so the loop could not advance on round 1.

Did NOT hand-author the missing envelope - writing a verification artifact by hand is mixed-mode drift and is forbidden. Took the sanctioned alternative instead: accepted all six Majors (none disputed), fixed them once, fixed four of five nits, answered the fifth, wrote s2-remediation-round-1.md, and re-ran --phase discovery on the corrected document. Within the 2-discovery-pass bound; regenerates the envelope through the blessed writer; and a full re-read is stronger than the fix-delta review it replaces, since a delta reviewer cannot see what already sits in its baseline (the failure that let two of S1 twelve Majors escape six rounds). Deviation recorded, not performed quietly.

Proved verification Major 4 rather than accepting it on argument: probed Windows PowerShell 5.1 native-stdout redirection on this machine and got first bytes ff fe - a UTF-16LE BOM. curl output redirected with > would reach persistence as UTF-16 and be rejected as malformed JSON, sending the reader to debug their own correct code. Switched to curl -o. Same evidence-first treatment as the earlier mkdir finding, which went the other way and was dismissed.

Discovery round 2 (fan-out 2/2, gpt-5-6) on the corrected document: four Majors and five nits in the merged envelope. Majors 1 and 3 are the same defect found independently by both arms - and it was introduced by round 1 own remediation: the fix for the hard-coded batch id put the capture in step 5, which meant step 5 called /run-now a second time after step 4 had already archived the only file. Found during a coherence read while round 2 was still running and fixed before the round returned; round 2 reviewed the pre-fix text. Third time in this set that remediation introduced a fresh defect (S1 recorded four).

All four Majors accepted, none disputed; all five nits fixed. Major 2 (ports never required by the build instructions, so a correct converter would fail every probe on 5101) fixed twice over: Listening on 5101/5102 added to the What to build lists, and --urls added to all five main-path dotnet run commands. Major 4 (reusing orders.csv collides in archive and returns AlreadyStored) fixed with a concrete Copy-Item to a unique name plus both consequences named. Nits: readback commands added to Parts B and C finish lines, the ScheduleEnabled poll race documented with its recovery, the cross-machine appendix corrected to bind BOTH services and carry the per-member database, and the too-categorical timeout-means-firewall claim rewritten. Wrote s2-remediation-round-2.md.

No build or code test applies: the session diff contains zero .py and zero .ts files - one new markdown tutorial plus session bookkeeping and raw routed artifacts. The relevant suite is the answer key it quotes, re-run today from D:/Projects/dabbler-csv-pipeline: 74 passing (31/24/19), 0 failed, 0 skipped. guidance_report --check OK at 10,895/12,000 tokens (91%). The repo pytest suite was started and had produced no output after 60+ minutes, so it was stopped; this session adds no Python to the package, so its count is inherited per the S1 precedent and cannot have been moved by this work.

Ran verify_session --phase remediation-review on the fix delta: VERIFIED, 0 findings, 3 fix verdicts accepted / 0 rejected (L3 recorded as duplicate-of L1). The reviewer additionally checked the new PowerShell flows, Part D outcome handling and cross-machine bindings for remediation-introduced blocking defects and found none. Loop closed inside the bounds: 2 discovery passes and 1 remediation-review cycle, no operator authorisation needed.
Authored disposition.json for S2 (preserving the patched verification fields), committed and pushed, ran close_session, then fired the session-complete notification.
Registered S3 via start_session (claude/anthropic/claude-opus-5/high). Read the preload, the spec, and the finished three-module-pipeline.md end to end.

R4 PRECONDITION SATISFIED BY READING, not by a link check: ownership routing landed in three-module-pipeline.md Step 4 'Route reviews by ownership' (lines 653-686), carrying both the GitHub CODEOWNERS form and the Azure DevOps 'Automatically included reviewers' equivalent. Only then was adopt-dabbler.md Part 5 eligible for deletion.

Trimmed adopt-dabbler.md to the single-module walk: deleted Part 5 (teammate + composing module) and Part 6 (review/merge/cleanup) entirely, 7461 chars; reframed the intro from 'two-module' to 'one person, one module' with a forward link; renumbered branch protection 'stage N of 3' -> 'of 2' (stage 3 lived in Part 5); repaired 'Parts 3-5' -> 'Parts 3-4' and the two prose forward-references to Part 5 inside Parts 2-3; rewrote the close as a five-item single-module check plus a 'Where to go next' section. 459 -> 333 lines.

git rm -r docs/tutorials/adopt-dabbler-video/ (9 files, operator-sanctioned in the spec). Its one live inbound link (adopt-dabbler.md:15, the 'On camera' bullet) was removed in the same pass, along with the 4 remaining *(scene N)* markers on the Part 1-4 headings; the Part 5/6 markers went with their parts. Set 107's activity log and change log mention the folder historically and were NOT touched.

Reconciled the inbound linkers. EDITED 5: README.md (dropped the now-false 'with a second module and a teammate added at the end', added the three-module tutorial as the next rung), docs/quick-start.md ('solo or as a small team' -> 'one person, one module' + new list entry), docs/module-reorganization.md (repointed 'hands-on team setup' at the new tutorial), docs/tutorials/module-team-hello-world.md (tombstone now routes the team half onward), docs/tutorials/release-and-recovery.md (names both upstream tutorials). NOT EDITED, deliberately: docs/tutorials/hello-world.md -- it makes no two-module promise, and tutorial_gate's _BANNED_TERMS forbids 'pipeline', 'repository' and 'teammate' in the first-run doc, so naming 'Three modules, one pipeline' there would turn CI red. The ladder still chains hello-world -> adopt-dabbler -> three-module.

Dead-link sweep: ZERO live references to adopt-dabbler-video/ outside session-set records; ZERO references to adopt-dabbler Parts 5/6; every surviving cross-doc citation (three-module-pipeline.md x6) targets Parts 1, 2-3 or 4, all of which survive. tutorial_gate.py's own links check passes.

Repaired a CI gate that was ALREADY RED on master at session start (commit be4d3b8, S2's close): tutorial_gate.py's _COMMAND_RE had no '.' in its character class, so it captured 'Dabbler: Open modules' from the correct text 'Dabbler: Open modules.yaml' and reported the repo's own tutorial as naming a non-existent command. 'Open modules.yaml' IS a real contributed command title. Fixed by allowing a dot only when a letter or digit follows (lookahead), so a dotted title is captured whole while a sentence-final period is not swallowed. Added 2 regression tests per L-069-1. Gate now exits 0; test_tutorial_gate.py 83 -> 85 passed. DISCLOSED for adjudication: outside the spec's S3 Touches list.

Appended the Session 3 block to ai-assignment.md; routed the next-orchestrator/next-set analysis via route(task_type='analysis', exclude anthropic) -> s3-ai-assignment-analysis.json. Rejected the analyst's engine 'bedrock' (not a repo engine; second consecutive session the analyst emitted an out-of-catalogue identifier). Adopted its structured walk-capture template for S4. Declined its Java-track next-set recommendation as premature by the spec's own non-goal ('after this one is walked'). Recommends claude/anthropic/claude-opus-5/high for S4, and the owed adopt-dabbler.md walk as the next set -- a debt this session materially enlarged.

Suite GREEN: 3143 passed, 6 skipped, 8 deselected in 48m55s (pytest -m 'not e2e', the invocation pytest.ini names as pre-commit). tutorial_gate.py exit 0; test_tutorial_gate.py 85 passed. An earlier full run was stopped at 35 min on the mistaken read that it had stalled -- it had not; the suite is just slow on Windows from git subprocess spawn. The e2e mark drives start_session/close_session against real git repos in tmpdirs and is unrelated to the Copilot seat.

verify_session --phase discovery: round 1, verdict VERIFIED, 0 blocking findings, two-way fan-out (both calls gpt-5-6; anthropic auto-excluded as the orchestrator's provider). Cost $0.4684. Eight nits across the two calls, none blocking. ACCEPTED AND FIXED post-round (both in text this session had touched): README's stale 'a reviewed pull request' promise -> 'a gated pull request' (the trimmed solo walk requires zero approvals), and the new regression test was fail-open -- it asserted only the absence of a violation, so it now asserts the capture equals 'Open modules.yaml' exactly. Gate + 85 tests re-run green after both. ADJUDICATED-MINOR, no change: the deleted video SCRIPT (never the tutorial) held the only active proof that a direct push to main is rejected -> re-homed to the owed adopt-dabbler walk; conventions block asserted results without pasting command output; 'creates nothing' meant product deliverables, not lifecycle machinery.

Registered session 4 (start_session, engine=claude/anthropic/claude-opus-5/high). Agreed the walk's staffing with the operator via AskUserQuestion, as spec Step 1 requires. Operator chose the FULL A-D walk performed by the orchestrator, acting as both the reader and the AI agent the tutorial tells the reader to hand the contract sections to. Rationale offered and accepted: the machine has .NET 10 SDK 10.0.201 and LocalDB MSSQLLocalDB present, so the walk is genuinely runnable here; the VS Code UI steps (Dabbler: New Module, plan/decomposition sets) are borrowed procedure the tutorial LINKS to adopt-dabbler.md rather than owning, so an orchestrator walk still covers nearly all of this tutorial's own material; and the cost lands on the Claude subscription rather than the very limited Copilot seat or the DABBLER_* keys. Declared gaps, to be recorded honestly in the walk evidence: the orchestrator is not a naive reader so reading-experience stalls are under-detected, and the extension UI steps are exercised only as file effects. Bonus scope accepted: solo Part D will ALSO be run against the published answer key's converter and persistence, which are a genuinely independent implementation, upgrading the solo claim from 'repoint mechanism' to real conformance.

Appended the Session 4 block to ai-assignment.md and routed the step-3.5 analysis (s4-ai-assignment-analysis.json, task_type=analysis, anthropic excluded). Recorded the walk-staffing decision and the two disciplines the walk binds itself to IN ADVANCE, both aimed at stopping the walk from producing evidence that flatters the document: CONTRACT-ONLY CONSTRUCTION (Parts A-C built from the tutorial's contract sections alone; the answer key's source is not opened until Part D, so anything the contract fails to state becomes a finding rather than a gap quietly filled from the reference solution) and STRICT COPY-PASTE (every command run exactly as printed; a failure is a document defect, never silently corrected). A third choice serves the same end: the walker's name is 'denmi', which appears nowhere in the tutorial -- its examples are 'priya' (team) and 'alex' (solo), so walking as either would silently pass any instruction that had accidentally hard-coded an example name. DEPARTURES FROM THE ANALYST: rejected its model ids as out of catalogue (claude-3-opus-20240229, gpt-4o) -- the THIRD consecutive session in which the step-3.5 analyst emitted an identifier this repo does not have (S3's was the engine 'bedrock'), now diagnosed and recorded as a follow-on rather than corrected one more time (the prompt asks for a model id but hands the analyst no catalogue, so it answers from training data older than the registry); declined its next_session_set (Increment B) in favour of the owed adopt-dabbler walk, because its weighting -- feature value over 'documentation debt' -- is wrong on these facts, the debt being that a document no human has ever followed end to end just lost a third of its content in S3; ADOPTED its third risk verbatim as the strict-copy-paste rule; adopted its first risk with a limit sharper than it knew -- this is the machine the tutorial was WRITTEN on, so the prerequisites section cannot be falsified here at all and is recorded as an explicit non-finding rather than a pass.

WALKED "Before you start" and "Day one" in a fresh repository at C:\temp\dabbler-108-walk, staged first into the exact state adopt-dabbler.md leaves a reader in -- a greeter module declared at services/greeter with its plan stub, committed as "chore: scaffold Dabbler and declare the greeter module" -- because this tutorial's own callout promises that module "will simply appear in the Work Explorer alongside the ones you are about to add", and that promise is only testable if the module is there.

PREREQUISITES: recorded as a NON-FINDING rather than a pass. dotnet --list-sdks and sqllocaldb info both returned what the tutorial prints, but this is the machine the tutorial was WRITTEN on -- the document literally reproduces this machine's SDK list -- so its prerequisite section cannot be falsified here at all. That limit was declared in advance in ai-assignment.md rather than discovered afterwards.

DEFECT FOUND -- THE SDK IS NOT PINNED (the walk's most consequential find so far). The tutorial's prerequisite check asks only for "a line beginning 10.0." and this machine satisfies it. But the machine also has 11.0.100-preview installed -- and the tutorial PRINTS that line in its own example output -- so `dotnet new web`, run as a reader would with no global.json, emitted <TargetFramework>net11.0</TargetFramework>. On a document titled "Three modules, one pipeline" whose every reference is .NET 10, a reader silently builds on a preview runtime. Severity is bounded by evidence rather than assumed: the bare net11.0 app BUILDS (0 warnings, 0 errors), so this is silent drift, not a hard break. Walked around it by adding global.json pinning 10.0.201 with rollForward latestFeature, after which dotnet new web emitted net10.0. Doc fix owed.

DEFECT FOUND -- THE DAY-ONE modules.yaml SNIPPET DROPS THE READER'S EXISTING MODULE. Step 3's YAML block opens at the `modules:` root key and lists only the three new entries, closing with the comment "# ...then Sam's three, then Chen's three". A reader who copy-pastes it as their file loses the greeter declaration that this same tutorial told them, 500 lines earlier, to leave alone. The surrounding prose does say the block shows "the shape", so a careful reader is fine -- but the document's own stated bar is that it is written for a reader with zero context, and this is precisely the kind of block that gets copied whole.

DAY ONE OTHERWISE HELD, and one part of it was verified against the shipping product rather than by eye. Simulated `Dabbler: New Module` three times in member-major order, writing exactly the entry the extension's renderModuleManifestEntry emits (codeRoots: [] plus its TODO comment), then hand-added the code roots as Step 3 instructs. The resulting docs/modules.yaml was then driven through the SHIPPING reader and grouping functions -- readModulesManifest, classifyModulesManifest, computeVisibleModules -- via a temporary mocha harness. Result: kind "present", four entries in manifest order (greeter, denmi-converter, denmi-persistence, denmi-watcher), all four rendering as `declared` flat rows with 0 sets and NO warnings. That is the tutorial's day-one output confirmed to render, not merely to look plausible, and it independently re-confirms the spec's POC finding that a day-one tree of empty declared modules is a healthy state. Step 4 (CODEOWNERS) was skipped exactly as the tutorial tells a solo reader to skip it.

The walker's name is `denmi`, which appears nowhere in the tutorial -- its examples are `priya` and `alex` -- so nothing here passed by accidentally matching an example.

WALKED PART A -- converter -- and it produced the strongest single piece of evidence in this walk.

METHOD, bound in advance: the module was built from the tutorial's Contract 1 section ALONE. The answer key's source was not opened. That is what makes the result below mean something.

THE HEADLINE RESULT: all three documented response bodies came back BYTE-IDENTICAL to the strings the tutorial prints, on the first run, with no iteration against them.
  - 200 envelope (379 chars) -- identical to the document's line 218.
  - 400 envelope (421 chars) -- identical to line 261.
  - unknown-schema 400 -- identical to line 275.
Compared programmatically against the literal document lines, not by eye. This is the tutorial's central premise -- that its contract sections are sufficient to build against -- falsifiable, tested, and held. Everything the document flags as easy to get wrong was in fact carried by the prose: the camelCase envelope with row keys passed through verbatim (OrderId, not orderId), the blank optional column arriving as an explicit null rather than a missing key, Amount preserving its written scale (250.00, not 250), rowCount excluding the header, and `line` counting physical file lines with the header as line 1.

FINISH LINE: all three items met. 29 tests green, first run, 1s (Failed: 0, Passed: 29, Skipped: 0). The tutorial's "for reference, the answer key has 31 tests -- an observation, not a target" landed exactly as designed: an independent build came out at 29, close enough to be reassuring and different enough to prove nothing was copied.

THE DOCUMENTED ESCAPE HATCH WORKS, AND WAS NEEDED. The finish-line command `dotnet run --project modules/denmi/converter --urls http://localhost:5101` FAILED as printed, because this build put its project under src/Converter -- which is the exact case the tutorial predicts. Its fallback (`Get-ChildItem -Recurse -Filter *.csproj modules/denmi/converter`) was run verbatim and printed a clear `Directory:` header naming the folder to pass to --project. That is a documented failure mode, correctly predicted and correctly remedied by the document itself, and it is worth recording as a PASS rather than a stall: the tutorial anticipated its own most likely first stumble.

GAPS IN THE CONTRACT, recorded as findings rather than quietly filled from the answer key. Contract 1 pins the four error messages its own examples exercise, but says nothing about the envelope for: a missing or extra header column (it states extras are rejected but shows no error shape), a violated `min` or `maxLength`, a non-integer OrderId, or a data row whose field count disagrees with the header. Each had to be invented here. None threatens Part D -- the watcher only reads the 4xx/5xx class -- but two independent implementations would produce different bodies for the same bad file, which is a real conformance gap in a document whose whole thesis is conformance.

WALKED PART B -- persistence -- built from Contract 2 alone, answer key still unopened.

FINISH LINE: all three items met. 29 tests green, first run, 2s (Failed: 0, Passed: 29, Skipped: 0) -- the same duration the tutorial quotes for the answer key's 24, and again a count close to but not equal to the reference, which is what the document says finished looks like.

CONTRACT FIDELITY, again exact. The documented 400 envelope came back BYTE-IDENTICAL to the tutorial's line 358 when driven with the batch its own example implies (schema "invoices", sourceFile "nope.csv", rowCount 2 against a one-row array). That makes FOUR documented response bodies now reproduced byte-for-byte from the contracts alone, across both services. The GET /batches/{id} view matched structurally on every point the contract calls out -- the casing flip to orderId on the way out, receivedAt as an offset timestamp, amount surviving SQL Server as 250.00 rather than 250, expedited round-tripping as an explicit null. The 201 carried a RELATIVE Location header, /batches/{the same id as the body}, exactly as documented.

THE DUPLICATE RULE, which the tutorial calls the point to check carefully, held on the first attempt. Running the tutorial's own PowerShell block verbatim gave duplicate False then True with the SAME batchId (019fc9f4-72b6-7b0a-829a-fe955b9dee29 both times). The tutorial's warning -- "if the second call returns a new GUID, your pipeline will double-load every file it ever retries" -- is the right thing to have flagged, and the unique index on sourceFile is what makes it fall out naturally.

A NOTE ON THE ID FORMAT THE DOCUMENT NEVER STATES, AND DID NOT NEED TO. Every batchId the tutorial prints begins 019fc8..., which is a UUIDv7. This build independently reached for Guid.CreateVersion7() and produced 019fc9f4..., the same shape. That is a happy accident rather than a contract term -- nothing in Contract 2 requires v7, and a conforming implementation using Guid.NewGuid() would print visibly different-looking ids. Worth recording only because a reader comparing their output against the document might wonder whether the resemblance is required. It is not.

DEFECT FOUND -- AN UNSTATED THIRD PREREQUISITE, and the walk nearly missed it for exactly the reason the step-3.5 analyst predicted. The tutorial's "What must be installed" names two things: the .NET 10 SDK and LocalDB. Part B then asks for "the database created and MIGRATED on start-up", and the natural EF Core reading of that is Database.Migrate(), which needs a migration, which needs `dotnet ef` -- a tool the .NET SDK does not ship. It ran here without complaint because this machine already has dotnet-ef 10.0.3 installed as a GLOBAL tool, which `dotnet tool list --global` confirms. A reader with only the two documented installs would hit "Could not execute because the specified command or file was not found" in the middle of Part B. The severity is genuinely conditional and is recorded as such: an agent that reaches for EnsureCreated() instead needs nothing extra, and the tutorial does not mandate migrations in so many words. This is the analyst's environment-contamination risk materialising precisely as forecast, caught only because the walk went looking for it.

ALSO OBSERVED, not a defect: the EF tools emitted "The Entity Framework tools version '10.0.3' is older than that of the runtime '10.0.10'" -- a warning, not an error, and the migration generated fine.

ONE PROBLEM IN THIS WALK WAS THE WALKER'S, NOT THE DOCUMENT'S, and is recorded so it is not miscounted as a finding: a shell heredoc collapsed the doubled backslash in the connection string, producing invalid JSON and an EF design-time failure. The tutorial's printed JSON at line 529 is correct; writing it exactly as printed worked immediately.

WALKED PART C -- watcher -- both phases. Built from the tutorial's decision table and the two contracts alone; answer key still unopened.

PHASE A, AND ITS CLAIM PROVEN RATHER THAN ASSERTED. 26 tests, 54 ms, covering all four rows of the decision table (Stored, AlreadyStored, Rejected, Deferred) plus the rule itself as theories over 400/404/422 and 500/502/503. The tutorial's claim is that this suite needs nothing running, so the walk did not merely assume it: BOTH SERVICES WERE STOPPED AND CONFIRMED DOWN by curl before the run, and the 26 tests then passed in 54 ms with no database, no file server and no other module started. That is negative test 2 of the spec's three, discharged with evidence rather than by inspection.

PHASE A ALSO EARNED ITS KEEP IMMEDIATELY, which is the best argument for it the walk could have produced. The first run was 25 passed / 1 FAILED: RunOnceAsync enumerated the incoming list while archiving mutated it, throwing "Collection was modified; enumeration operation may not execute."
